items.abstract: <jats:p>Natural Language Generation (NLG) has improved exponentially in recent years thanks to the development of sequence-to-sequence deep learning technologies such as Transformer-based language models. This advancement has led to more fluent and coherent NLG, leading to improved development in downstream tasks such as abstractive summarization, dialogue generation, and data-to-text generation. However, it is also apparent that deep learning based generation is prone to hallucinate unintended text, which degrades the system performance and fails to meet user expectations in many real-world scenarios. To address this issue, many studies have been presented in measuring and mitigating hallucinated texts, but these have never been reviewed in a comprehensive manner before.</jats:p><jats:p>In this survey, we thus provide a broad overview of the research progress and challenges in the hallucination problem in NLG. The survey is organized into two parts: (1) a general overview of metrics, mitigation methods, and future directions, and (2) an overview of task-specific research progress on hallucinations in the following downstream tasks, namely abstractive summarization, dialogue generation, generative question answering, data-to-text generation, and machine translation. This survey serves to facilitate collaborative efforts among researchers in tackling the challenge of hallucinated texts in NLG.</jats:p><jats:p/>

title: Hallucination in Large Language Models and Retrieval-Augmented Generation: Mechanisms, Mitigation, and Evaluation
items.abstract: <jats:p>Large language models have demonstrated strong generative capability in question answering, dialogue, and other knowledge-intensive tasks. However, their outputs remain vulnerable to hallucination, including factual errors, unsupported claims, spurious citations, and distorted reasoning. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) has been proposed as a practical remedy because it supplements parametric knowledge with external evidence retrieved at inference time. Yet RAG does not guarantee truthfulness or attribution by default. Errors may arise during query formulation, document retrieval, evidence aggregation, and answer grounding. This paper reviews the relationship between hallucination and RAG from three perspectives: mechanism, mitigation, and evaluation. First, the major causes of hallucination in both vanilla LLMs and RAG-enhanced systems are analyzed. Second, the principal mitigation strategies are organized into retrieval optimization, evidence-grounded generation, and post-generation verification. Third, the main evaluation dimensions are examined, including factuality, faithfulness, attribution quality, and retrieval relevance. It is argued that RAG should not be treated as a complete solution to hallucination. Its value lies in enabling externally grounded generation, but its effectiveness depends on the reliability of retrieval, the fidelity of evidence use, and the rigor of evaluation. Future work should prioritize attribution-aware generation, conflict-sensitive reasoning, and unified evaluation protocols for trustworthy LLM systems.</jats:p>

title: Natural Language Processing: Foundations and Applications without Hallucination from Generative AI
items.abstract:
<jats:p><p><span>This research note takes readers on a visual, step-by-step journey into how AI reads the meaning behind words, not just the words themselves. Using algebra and geometry, it builds sentence similarity in five steps: contrasting keyword matching with meaning matching; representing sentences as vectors of numbers; deriving the dot product from the Pythagorean theorem; generalizing to cosine similarity via the Law of Cosines; and extending the idea from two dimensions to the hundreds used by embedding models that power modern semantic search, chatbots, and AI agents.</span></p>
<p><span>The note's central payoff is a chatbot architecture without hallucination from generative AI. Large language models (LLMs) generate text word by word—the mechanism behind their fluent but sometimes fabricated answers. A system built on sentence similarity works differently: it is <b>selective</b>, not <b>generative</b>. It returns only a sentence that already exists in a verified document or says <b>“I don't know”</b> when no candidate clears a similarity threshold. This differs from retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), which narrows hallucination but does not eliminate it, since the LLM still combines retrieved text with pre-trained knowledge.</span></p>
<p><span>By opening this black box with plain English and visuals rather than code, the note equips non-technical readers to engage critically with the AI systems they rely on: what these systems are trained on and why a system that always answers, however unrelated the question, should be treated with caution. In high-stakes fields, the AI systems worth trusting are not the ones that always have an answer, but the ones that know when to say “I don't know.”</span></p></jats:p>
